title: 5 Reasons My Class Begins With Retrieval Practice (Almost) Daily most-daily/
author: Blake Harvard
summary: Blake Harvard explains why he has opened class with a brief retrieval-practice review almost every day for six or seven years. First, it creates a predictable routine that absorbs the uncertain, behaviour-prone opening minutes of class while the teacher handles administrative tasks like attendance. Second, it exploits the well-documented testing effect: retrieving information from memory strengthens it far more than passive study methods like rereading or highlighting, which students tend to prefer despite being less effective. Third, spacing that retrieval, reviewing today's content again tomorrow rather than only before a summative test, produces more durable long-term learning than cramming, even though cramming can produce misleading short-term gains. Fourth, daily retrieval confronts students with their own overconfidence, since most forgetting happens in the first day or two after initial learning, and Harvard argues reframing forgetting as universal and normal, rather than as a personal failing, matters for how students respond to it. Fifth, the daily practice itself models good study habits by giving students repeated experience with retrieval and spacing, techniques they wouldn't otherwise choose to use on their own, since the whole point is to show them, not just tell them, how effective studying actually works.
points: Harvard's first reason is non-academic: the daily retrieval routine absorbs an uncertain, behaviour-prone opening period, freeing the teacher to handle administrative tasks like attendance while establishing a consistent start-of-class expectation.

He grounds the exercise in the testing effect, the century-plus of research showing retrieval strengthens memory more than passive study methods like rereading or highlighting that students tend to prefer.

He argues most forgetting happens within the first day or two of initial learning, which is why next-day retrieval specifically (not just eventual review before a test) is positioned as the critical intervention point.

He explicitly reframes forgetting as universal and normal rather than a personal failing, arguing that daily retrieval practice softens the sting of discovering gaps by normalising the experience of not remembering everything.
quotes: For the past six or seven years I have started my class (almost) every day the same way, with retrieval practice.
If students know they are to come in and immediately begin on this review, a lot of the nonsense that may present itself is immediately squashed.
The act of retrieving information (also called the testing effect) from memory has over a century of research pointing to its positive impact on learning.
Spacing out the retrieval practice of material is much more likely to produce more permanent changes in long-term memory.
In fact, most of our forgetting occurs in the first day or two after we’ve experienced new material.
We need to reframe how we talk to students about forgetting. Let them know it is normal but also show them strategies that help to curtail the forgetting.
